title: Bishop and knight I: the W manoeuvre
summary: From the wrong corner to the right one, with the knight drawing a W.
part.wrongCorner.title: The wrong corner
part.wrongCorner.summary: Why the mate only exists in the corner of the bishop's colour, and the first point of the W.
part.theW.title: The W to the end
part.theW.summary: The knight takes the dark squares of the eighth rank one by one, until the king reaches c8.
part.detours.title: Escapes and the mate
part.detours.summary: The punishment for running back to the wrong corner, Rhine's trap and the final mate.
part.wRules.title: Rules and practice
part.wRules.summary: The stalemate alarm, three rules and the whole W in the practical challenge.
step.t_corner: The black king is already on the edge, on h8. Before any move: in which corner can this mate happen, and which piece will take the dark squares of the eighth rank?
step.t_corner.hint1: Compare the colour of h8 with the colour of your bishop's squares. The mate only exists in the corner of the bishop's colour.
step.corner: This is the mate that embarrasses masters the most. De la Villa tells of players who went home with their heads down for not knowing it. Look at the position: the black king is already on the edge, huddled in h8. It looks almost over, but h8 is a dark square and your bishop only walks on light ones. That is the wrong corner. The mate only exists in the corner of the bishop's colour: a8 or h1. Our journey is to take the king from h8 to a8, along the eighth rank. Remember: the squares and moves highlighted in what I say, like h8, can be tapped; tap one and I will show it on the board.
step.whyWrong: Why does the corner matter? Look at the finished mate in the right corner. The black king on a8, a light square. Your king on b6 takes a7 and b7, the knight on a6 takes b8, and the bishop gives check along the long diagonal. Everything fits. In the dark corner the bishop reaches neither the king nor the corner square, and too much is left for the knight: from there the mate cannot be forced. So we empty the wrong corner and close the right one.
step.wShape: Now the secret, which Philidor already pointed out in 1777: the knight's path. On the eighth rank the dark squares are h8, f8, d8 and b8, and those are the ones the black king needs. The knight will take them one by one: f7, e5, d7, c5, b7. Draw it on the board and you will see a W. Each point of the W takes a dark square; the bishop does the rest on the light ones. Let us play this W together, move by move.
step.w1: First point of the W. The king is on h8 and your knight on e5. Take h8 from him, with check.
step.w1.hint: The knight from e5 gives check on the square that also covers h8. Look on the seventh rank.
step.w1.done: 1.Nf7+. The king has only g8, and h8 is gone for good. First point done.
step.w2: The king went to g8 and wants to come back. The next square to take is g8, a light one: the bishop's job. The bishop is already on the diagonal, but 1.Bh7+ right now would be captured. First a waiting move along the diagonal, then bring it to h7, and when the king steps onto e8, bring the knight back to the centre, on e5. Three moves of yours.
step.w2.hint: 1.Bh7+ now loses the bishop. Wait with it on f5, on the same diagonal: the king is forced to f8. After 2.Bh7 the king goes to e8 and the knight returns to e5, where it covers d7.
step.w2.done: 1.Bf5, 2.Bh7 and 3.Ne5. The king has lost h8 and g8 and stands on e8, and the knight already covers d7, the door to the centre. Second point of the W.
step.w3: The black king stepped onto d8 and will try to escape along the seventh rank: c7, then b6 or c5. First bring your king to e6, to take d7 and e7. When he goes to c7, the third point of the W, on d7, takes b6 and c5 from him.
step.w3.hint: King to e6 first. After the black king reaches c7, the knight jumps from e5 to d7 and covers b6 and c5.
step.w3.done: 1.Ke6 and 2.Nd7. The king went to c7, but look at what he has: b6 and b8 belong to the knight, d6 and d7 to you. Third point.
step.w4: The black king is on b7 and looks at c6, from where he wants to reach b5 and c4. Before he gets out, close both squares with the bishop, in one move.
step.w4.hint: One square on the b1–h7 diagonal covers b5 and c4 at the same time. The bishop goes back the way it came.
step.w4.done: 1.Bd3. Now the black king goes to c6 and stops: b5 and c4 belong to the bishop, b6, c5 and d7 to the knight and your king. The net is closed.
step.w5: The black king is on c6 with no way out. You need to pass the move to him without letting anything go. The bishop does that: a waiting move along the diagonal, and on the next move it takes the long diagonal, a8–h1, its home until the mate.
step.w5.hint: Bishop to e2, waiting; the black king returns to c7. Then bishop to f3, on the long diagonal.
step.w5.done: 1.Be2 and 2.Bf3. The black king can no longer stay on the seventh and goes back to the eighth. Notice: the bishop on f3 covers b7, the square where the black king would love to sit.
step.w6: Now the final push along the eighth. The black king is on d8. Take d6 with your king; he goes to e8, trying the far side. Chase him off with a bishop check on h5, and bring the bishop to f7, where it covers e8 and g8. Then the knight makes the last two points of the W: c5 and b7 with check. Five moves of yours.
step.w6.hint: 1.Kd6, then 2.Bh5+ and 3.Bf7. With the bishop on f7, the knight goes from d7 to c5 and from c5 to b7 with check.
step.w6.done: 1.Kd6, 2.Bh5+, 3.Bf7, 4.Nc5 and 5.Nb7+. The W is complete: f7, e5, d7, c5, b7. The black king is stuck on c8 and can only go to b8. Only the mate is left.
step.t_escape: The black king tries to run back to the wrong corner, eyeing g8 and h8. How do you punish that and take both squares from it at once?
step.t_escape.hint1: Look for a knight check that also covers f8. Then your king shuts the seventh rank.
step.escape: Go back a little. After 2.Bh7 and 2...Ke8, not every king goes to d8. Some try to return to the wrong corner: 3...Kf8, eyeing g8 and h8. Karttunen beat Rasik that way in 2003, punishing every retreat. Punish this one: knight check, and the white king takes e6.
step.escape.hint: The knight from e5 gives check on d7 and at the same time covers f8. After 1...Ke8, your king goes to e6.
step.escape.done: 1.Nd7+ and 2.Ke6. The black king lost f8 and g8 at once, and your king is already on e6. Going back to the wrong corner only shortens his road.
step.trap: Near the right corner lives a trap, found by Frederick Rhine in 2000. White to play, and 1.Nb6+ looks natural: check, and the king goes to b7, doesn't it? No. The king goes to d8 and attacks the bishop on e8. Now every bishop move leaves the black king without a move: stalemate. And any other move loses the bishop, and king and knight cannot mate. Draw. Rule: near the corner, before every knight check, see whether the bishop is safe and whether the black king still has a square.
step.finish: The W is done. The black king is on c8, the knight on b7, the bishop on f7. Now the mate: bring your king to c6 and b6, give a bishop check on e6 when the black king is on c8, bring the knight to c5, wait with the bishop on d7, and close with 6.Na6+ and 7.Bc6. Seven moves, and no stalemate on the way.
step.finish.hint: 1.Kc6 and 2.Kb6 first. The black king on c8 gets 3.Be6+. Then 4.Nc5, a waiting 5.Bd7, 6.Na6+ and the mate with the bishop on c6.
step.finish.done: Checkmate. King on b6, knight on a6, bishop on c6: the pattern we saw at the start. You took the king from the wrong corner to the right one and shut the door.
step.t_stalemate: The black king is in the right corner and the mate is close. But the natural-looking move draws. What is the safe way to the mate?
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Before each move, count the black king's squares. No square and no check is stalemate: sometimes the bishop has to wait.
step.rules: Three rules to take into your games. First: the mate is in the corner of the bishop's colour; if the king is in the other one, the journey goes along the edge. Second: the knight takes the dark squares of the edge in a W: f7, e5, d7, c5, b7; the bishop takes the light ones and gives the final check. Third: near the corner, before every knight check, check for stalemate and for the bishop. Now you play.
step.playW: The whole W position. The black king on h8, the wrong corner. Take him to a8 and mate. No hurry: the fifty-move rule is generous to those who know the way.
step.playFar: A little further out. The knight is still on d3 and the black king on g8. Build the W first: knight to e5, king to f6, knight to f7. Then the road you already know.
ex.e13: White to play and mate. The black king is on a7, next to the right corner, and your king already takes b8, b7 and b6. Two knight checks look possible. Which one pushes the king to a8 without opening another door?
ex.e13.hint: Look at your bishop's diagonal, from f1 to a6. One of the knight checks blocks that diagonal with its own piece.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Nc8+! forces 1...Ka8: a6 belongs to the bishop, b6 to the knight and the king, and from c8 the knight also takes a7. Then 2.Bg2 is mate along the long diagonal. The other check, 1.Nb5+, blocks the f1–a6 diagonal with the knight, and the black king escapes to a6. It is a mating net the lesson did not show: king on c7 and knight on c8, instead of king on b6 and knight on a6.
ex.e14: White to play and win. Ushenina against Girya, Geneva 2013. The black king is on a1, a dark corner, and your bishop is light-squared: the mate has to be on h1. Now the W runs along the first rank. Bring the knight to the first point. Two moves of yours.
ex.e14.hint: In the lesson, the first point took h8 from the king. Here the square to take is a1, and from d1 the knight cannot get there in one jump: it needs a stepping stone.
ex.e14.solution: 77.Ne3! Kb1 78.Nc2, as Ushenina played. From c2 the knight takes a1 and e1, the dark edge squares near the black king: it is the first point of the W, the same idea as 1.Nf7 in the lesson, now on the first rank. She went on with 79.Ba2, which takes b1 as 2.Bh7 took g8, and 80.Nd4, the second point. The stumble came later.
ex.e15: White to play and win. The knight on b8 is attacked by the black king, and mate is close. Only one move wins: save the knight without stalemating the king.
ex.e15.hint: If the knight leaves b8, the black king has no move. If the bishop moves, the knight falls, and king and bishop cannot mate. One piece is left to move.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Kc7! defends the knight and gives a7 back to the black king. After 1...Ka7, 2.Bc8! takes the bishop behind the knight, 2...Ka8, 3.Bb7+ Ka7 and 4.Nc6 is mate: the king on c7 takes b8, b7 and b6, the bishop on b7 is protected by the king and takes a8, and the knight gives the check. 1.Nc6 or 1.Nd7 on the first move stalemate the black king, and any other move lets the knight fall.
ex.e17: White to play and win. Karttunen against Rasik, European Club Cup, 2003. The bishop is dark-squared and the mate will be on h8. The W was going well, but the black king slipped off the edge to f6. Send the king back to the eighth rank and squeeze him again. Three moves of yours.
ex.e17.hint: A bishop check now lets the black king go down to g5. First close the squares on the way down with a quiet bishop move; then the bishop returns to the long diagonal. When the black king is back on the eighth rank, choose: squeeze with the king or with the bishop?
ex.e17.solution: 93.Be3! takes g5 and f4; the knight on e7 already takes f5 and g6, and your king takes e5 and e6. The black king has to go back: 93...Kf7. Then 94.Bd4 (94.Bg5, 94.Bf4 and 94.Kd7 also work) closes the road again, and the black king returns to the eighth rank: 94...Ke8. Now 95.Ke6!, with the king and not the bishop: your king takes d7 and f7, and the black king can only walk along the eighth rank. Karttunen played all three moves. The check 93.Bd4+ on the first move looks more natural, but lets the king go to g5; and 95.Bb6 on the last one, defending the knight, also takes longer.
ex.e18: White to play and win. Another road after the third point of the W, from Seirawan's line quoted on Wikipedia: black king on c7, knight on d7, bishop on c4. Lock the king in the a8 corner without the W to b7. Three moves of yours.
ex.e18.hint: The knight on d7 is attacked and only your king defends it. Give it a second defender that also takes c6 from the black king. Then the knight finds, by another road, the central square from which it takes b6 and c7 at once.
ex.e18.solution: 1.Bb5! defends the knight and takes c6 and a6 (1.Bd5 also works, a little slower). After 1...Kd8, the knight leaves d7 (2.Nf6, as Seirawan played; 2.Nc5, 2.Ne5 and 2.Nb6 come to the same; 2.Kd6 also wins) and, when the king returns to c7, 3.Nd5+ sends him back to the eighth rank: from d5 the knight takes b6, c7 and e7. The black king is locked in the a8 corner, and the mate follows with Kd6 and Ke7.
ex.e19: White to play and win. Ushenina against Girya, Geneva 2013, later on. The black king went towards the wrong corner, h8, and now the W runs down the h-file, to h1, your bishop's corner. Five moves of yours; the last one is the move the world champion missed.
ex.e19.hint: Start with the bishop: seal the black king behind the a2–g8 diagonal and then the bishop takes from the king the light square on the h-file he still has. The knight returns to the centre and the king follows. At the end, the black king wants to get out through f2 and e3: one knight jump closes both.
ex.e19.solution: 103.Be6! Kh6, 104.Bg8! Kh5 (the bishop takes h7 and holds the a2–g8 diagonal), 105.Ne5 Kh4 (the knight takes g4 and g6), 106.Kf5 (or a waiting bishop move, 106.Bd5 or 106.Bb3) Kg3 and 107.Ng4! The knight takes f2, e3 and h2, and the black king is locked in the h1 corner. In the game, Ushenina played 107.Bc4? instead of 107.Ng4, the black king escaped through f2 and the game ended in a draw by the fifty-move rule. 107.Bb3 also wins, only more slowly.
key.wStart: The black king hides in the wrong corner, the one the bishop can't reach. From here the W manoeuvre begins, taking it to the right corner.
key.mateCorner: Mate in the right corner: the bishop checks along the diagonal, and the knight and king take the last squares.
key.rhineTrap: A stalemate trap: a hasty knight check leaves the bishop stuck next to the black king. Any bishop move stalemates, and anything else loses the bishop.
key.escapeBack: The black king tries to run back to the wrong corner, but a knight check pushes it back towards the right one.
key.stalemateAlert: Close to mate, careful: one careless knight move leaves the black king with no move at all, and it's stalemate. The bishop waits for the moment of the final check.
history: With bishop and knight, mate is only possible in a corner of the same colour as the bishop. A good defender runs to the other corner, the wrong one, and you need to know how to get him out. That's what the W manoeuvre is for: the knight zigzags, drawing a W on the board, while the king and bishop push the black king along the edge to the right corner. The first to describe this route was the Frenchman François-André Philidor, the strongest player of the eighteenth century, in 1777. The ending is rare, so some teachers skip it, but grandmasters have lost half a point for not knowing it: Anna Ushenina, women's world champion, could only draw against Olga Girya in Geneva in 2013.
practice: Now the real endgame. In this position the black king is near h1, the right corner for your bishop: close the net and mate without stalemating. Pick a pace and challenge the clock, or set up your own training.
